::: {.letter-metadata}
**Date:** Oct 14th [1852]  
**From:** Otterbourn  
**Manuscript:** MS Huntington Library: Yonge Letters
:::

Dear [Madam](people/person_1243.qmd),
It was Edward I who made the law for planting yew trees in Church yards, at least so I was told by a gentleman who never makes mistakes, and is deeply read in history.[^1] I have looked in vain in [Evelyn’s silva](other_books/otherbook_61.qmd) and [Loudon’s arboretum](other_books/otherbook_109.qmd), but I think his information to be trusted. He says it had been done long before, but it was only in Edwd I’s reign that it became the subject of a statute. We have a Ch yard yew near us of very great age, and cut exactly into the shape of a mushroom. I have ventured to erase your ‘alas!’ to St Leonard, for a happy death hardly seems to me a subject for that interjection. I also took out the direct reference to [Dr Newman](people/person_1084.qmd)’s Sermons. I like the beautiful quotation of that very fine sermon but I had rather not acknowledge it.[^2] They have made some strange misprints in the botanical names, but I have not the right ones at hand, and so have left them for you. Your November verses are much too pretty to spare any of them, I will take care they come in at any rate in this next number. I am sorry we are so near the end of the [Garland](other_books/otherbook_225.qmd). I have enjoyed it so much on my own account, but I must look forward to [Margaret and her mother](other_books/otherbook_234.qmd). I conclude that you are at Helmington again and direct there

Yours sincerely
C M Yonge

---

[^1]: The statute ‘Ne Rector prosternat arbores in Caemeterio’ is said to have been passed in 1307.
[^2]: This was because Newman had become a Roman Catholic and *[MP](organizations/other_52.qmd)* did not want the reputation of encouraging conversion.
